newsitem.title: GERMANY: "Mr Financial Markets" takes helm at Deutsche.
newsitem.headline: "Mr Financial Markets" takes helm at Deutsche.

text.p: Rolf Breuer, an eloquent investment banker who has spearheaded the modernisation of Germany's financial centre, takes on one of the most powerful posts in European business on Tuesday when he succeeds Hilmar Kopper as head of Deutsche Bank AG.

Breuer, 59, known here as "Mr Financial Markets," will guide Deutsche into the next millennium in pursuit of Kopper's ambition to forge a bank that is Number One in Europe and among the top players worldwide.

Deutsche, Germany's largest bank with net assets of around 900 billion marks ($500 billion), has made big strides towards that goal since Kopper became chief executive in 1989 after his predecessor Alfred Herrhausen was murdered by guerrillas.
Breuer is inheriting a bank which has doubled in size, built up a powerful London-based investment bank and reorganised its domestic branch network in the last 7 years.
Kopper, 62, will move up to become chairman of the bank's non-executive supervisory board at the end of Tuesday's annual shareholders' meeting.
"I think Kopper's role will be very positively judged in retrospect," said Stefan Ermisch, banking analyst at Westdeutsche Landesbank in Duesseldorf.
"Breuer will take steps to boost shareholder value but I do not expect him to make major changes to the bank's strategy as Kopper defined it."
Breuer joined Deutsche as a trainee in 1956 and has been on its management board since 1985, most recently as one of three three top executives in charge of investment banking.

It will be up to Breuer, a cosmopolitan Anglophile who looks 10 years younger than his age, to preside over Deutsche's transition to monetary union and steer the bank through inevitable consolidation in the domestic banking scene.
He also faces the task of boosting returns from Deutsche's cost-laden domestic branch network.

Many analysts believe that by the year 2000 Germany's top five banks will have merged to become the top three. Deutsche itself provoked merger speculation in the sector last July by announcing it had bought a 5.21 percent stake in Munich-based rival Bayerische Vereinsbank AG.
Deutsche Bank's expansion drive has not been plain sailing.
The bank, whose size and large portfolio of industrial shareholdings frequently expose it to public criticism of perceived excessive banking power, has weathered a series of setbacks in recent years.
It has been involved in major corporate collapses, most notably the near-bankruptcy of metals group Metallgesellschaft AG in 1993 and the meltdown of the Schneider real estate group in 1994.

And only last month it was fined a record two million pounds ($3.3 million) for irregularities by fund manager Peter Young at its British fund arm Morgan Grenfell Asset Management. Compensating investors and shoring up the unit trusts involved cost Deutsche up to 1.2 billion marks.

Breuer's smoother style is expected to help project a less abrasive image for the bank than the outspoken and sometimes blunt Kopper, whose infamous "peanuts" remark seems destined to stick with Deutsche long after his retirement.

In an off-the-cuff remark in 1994, Kopper sparked public outrage by dismissing as "peanuts" 50 million marks of trade debts left by real estate magnate Juergen Schneider, whose empire crumbled after he abandoned it.
The plan to reduce German shareholdings could also help silence calls for curbs on the power banks wield through their stakes and representation on company supervisory boards.

But Breuer had his first taste of controversy in March when Deutsche backed an abortive hostile takeover bid by steelmaker Krupp AG for Thyssen AG, a move which prompted 30,000 angry steelworkers to besiege Deutsche's Frankfurt headquarters.

While he welcomed the Anglo-Saxon style bid as enhancing Germany's reputation as a financial centre, politicians and unions were outraged at the bank's support for "Wild West" style American capitalism.
Despite his new responsibilities, Breuer is not expected to cease his crusade to get Frankfurt in shape to rival London as financial centre.
He is widely credited with helping to transform Germany from a crusty haven for insider traders into a modern financial centre.

In his capacity as head of the supervisory board of stock exchange holding company Deutsche Boerse AG, he never tires of exhorting fellow bankers to adopt Anglo-Saxon concepts of shareholder value, transparency and investor relations. ($ = 1.695 German Marks) ($ = 0.608 British Pounds)
